chunks: Why multiple supply voltages. The question: Why are multiple supply voltages needed?
Different parts of a chip want different supply voltages. A lower voltage saves a lot of power, so parts that do not need top speed should get a lower one.
Some circuits need their own voltage anyway, such as memory cells, input/output pins and analog circuits (which handle smooth, non-digital signals).
A part with its own supply can also be switched off when idle.
The costs are extra regulators (circuits that make each voltage) and extra circuits to pass signals between voltage levels.
Think of heating a house. You could heat every room to the warmest temperature anyone wants, but that wastes fuel. Giving each room its own thermostat saves energy.
A greenhouse wants warm, a pantry cool. The cost is more heaters and more care where rooms meet.
One difference: chip power grows with voltage squared, so the savings are larger than with heat.
A typical SoC has separately controlled rails for CPU, GPU, memories, always-on logic, I/O, analog and DRAM. Each rail has its own voltage range and its own regulator in the PMIC.
Rail: one supply line held at a fixed voltage. Voltage domain: a region of the chip with its own supply voltage.
Level shifter: a circuit that translates a signal from one voltage level to another. Isolation cell: a circuit that holds a switched-off domain's output at a safe value.
LDO: a simple regulator that burns the extra voltage off as heat. Buck converter: an efficient switching regulator that steps voltage down with little loss.
Say 30% of a chip's switching circuits sit on the slowest paths and need 1. 0 volts to keep up with the clock. The other 70% keep up at 0. 8 volts. On one 1.
0 volts rail, relative power is 1. 000. With two rails, it is 0. 3 times 1. 0 plus 0. 7 times 0. 8 squared equals 0. 748 , a 25% saving. The regulator matters too.
An LDO making 0. 8 volts from 1. 0 volts saves only 20% at its input, while a buck converter at 90% efficiency saves about 29%. That is the whole idea.
